title: How many turns fit for each shape in the first row?
description: The first row of shapes in the table of Chapter one has a triangle, a square, a pentagon and so on up to a decagon, each with equal sides and equal angles. Turning each one about its centre gives its angles of symmetry, and the counts form a number pattern. The video checks that the full turn is counted, so the triangle has three turns and not two.
teaching_notes: One idea: a shape with all sides equal and all angles equal fits after a turn of three hundred sixty divided by its number of sides, so it has as many angles of symmetry as sides. Watch for students who leave out the full turn and count one fewer.

source: Figure it Out Q9 (section 9.2, second block)
video_script.why: The child finds the smallest turn that fits for a regular polygon, lists all its angles of symmetry including the full turn, and sees that the count equals the number of sides.
video_script.substitution: Pin each paper shape at its centre, turn it, and count every turn at which it fits its own outline, including the full turn.
video_script.anchor: the first row of shapes in the table of Chapter 1: a triangle, a square, a pentagon, a hexagon, a heptagon, an octagon, a nonagon and a decagon, each with equal sides and equal angles
video_script.payoff_line: Each shape has as many angles of symmetry as it has sides

final_answer.spoken: three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, which are the counting numbers starting from three

never_show: a triangle shown with only 2 angles of symmetry
the full turn left out of a list of turns
maths_rules: a regular polygon with n sides fits itself after each turn of 360 / n degrees, so it has n angles of symmetry, counting 360
the sequence for the triangle up to the decagon is 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, the counting numbers starting from 3
slip: the full turn of 360 degrees always fits and is counted, so the triangle has 3 angles, not 2
video_script.design: One idea: the smallest turn that fits is 360 divided by the number of sides, and every multiple of it fits too. Shapes appear one after the other in the order of the book's table. Turns are amber and the centre dot is red.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about a row of shapes in Chapter one.
<bookmark mark='row'/>The row goes from a triangle on the left to a shape with ten sides on the right.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many turns about the centre make each shape fit, and what pattern do the numbers make?

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

narration: <bookmark mark='reg'/>A shape with all sides equal and all angles equal is called a regular polygon. Every shape in the row is one.
<bookmark mark='angle'/>A turn about the centre that makes the shape look the same is called an angle of symmetry.
<bookmark mark='full'/>A full turn always fits, so three hundred sixty degrees is always one of the angles.

beats.on_screen: Given: eight regular polygons, with 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 sides

marks.given: the numbers of sides of the eight shapes are written under them

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, there are eight regular polygons, and they have from three up to ten sides.

beats.on_screen: To find: the angles of symmetry of each shape, and the pattern of the numbers

marks.find: the words angles of symmetry and pattern are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the angles of symmetry of each shape, and then the pattern of the numbers.

beats.on_screen: Step 1, the triangle: 360 / 3 = 120; turns 120, 240, 360 degrees; 3 angles

marks.tri: the triangle turns about its red centre dot and first fits after a third of a full turn
marks.list: the turns 120, 240 and 360 degrees are listed in amber and counted as three angles

narration: <bookmark mark='tri'/>Step one, turn the triangle about its centre. It first fits after a third of a full turn.
<bookmark mark='deg'/>Three hundred sixty divided by three is one hundred twenty degrees.
<bookmark mark='list'/>It fits at one hundred twenty, two hundred forty and three hundred sixty degrees. That is three angles.

beats.on_screen: Step 2, the square: 360 / 4 = 90; turns 90, 180, 270, 360 degrees; 4 angles

marks.sq: the square turns about its red centre dot and first fits after a quarter of a full turn
marks.list: the turns 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees are listed in amber and counted as four angles

narration: <bookmark mark='sq'/>Step two, turn the square about its centre. It first fits after a quarter of a full turn.
<bookmark mark='deg'/>Three hundred sixty divided by four is ninety degrees.
<bookmark mark='list'/>It fits at ninety, one hundred eighty, two hundred seventy and three hundred sixty degrees. That is four angles.

beats.on_screen: Step 3, the hexagon: 360 / 6 = 60; turns 60, 120, 180, 240, 300, 360 degrees; 6 angles

marks.hex: the hexagon turns about its red centre dot and first fits after a sixth of a full turn
marks.list: the turns 60, 120, 180, 240, 300 and 360 degrees are listed in amber and counted as six angles

narration: <bookmark mark='hex'/>Step three, turn the hexagon about its centre. It first fits after a sixth of a full turn.
<bookmark mark='deg'/>Three hundred sixty divided by six is sixty degrees.
<bookmark mark='list'/>Each new fit is sixty degrees more. The last one is the full turn, so there are six angles.

beats.on_screen: Step 4, the pattern: every shape has as many angles as sides, so the numbers go up by one each time

marks.rest: the pentagon, the heptagon, the octagon, the nonagon and the decagon turn the same way, each with the full turn counted
marks.up: the numbers of angles are listed in a row with a plus one arrow between each pair
marks.name: the words the counting numbers starting from three are written under the row

narration: <bookmark mark='rest'/>Step four, the other shapes turn the same way. Each one has as many angles as it has sides.
<bookmark mark='up'/>The numbers go up by one each time.
<bookmark mark='name'/>These are the counting numbers, starting from three.

beats.on_screen: Step 5, check: turn the triangle again and count the fits, including the full turn; the angles equal the sides

marks.check: the triangle turns 120, 240 and 360 degrees and the three fits are counted
marks.all: a tick appears beside each shape where the angles equal the sides

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step five, put the answer back in the question. Turn the triangle again and count the fits, and the full turn makes three.
<bookmark mark='all'/>For every shape in the row, the angles equal the sides.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10: the counting numbers starting from 3

marks.nums: the numbers are ticked off one by one

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Each shape has as many angles of symmetry as it has sides.
<bookmark mark='nums'/>The numbers are the counting numbers from three.
They are three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine and ten.
